nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What is widely believed to have contributed to the recovery of benthic invertebrate assemblages in Europe?
nodes.answer: The recovery is widely believed to have primarily resulted from improvements in water quality.
nodes.paragraph: Ecological Processes (2025) 14:30 It is widely believed that the recovery of benthic inver - tebrate assemblages in Europe has primarily resulted from improvements in water quality (Haase et al. 2023; Sinclair et al. 2024). While water quality enhancements have undoubtedly played a crucial role, the relationship between these improvements and broader ecological out - comes is more complex than it might appear, especially at larger scales. This complexity raises critical questions about additional factors that influence ecological recov - ery. For instance, hydromorphological restoration pro - jects, which aim to restore physical habitat conditions, have shown varying degrees of success (Kail et al. 2015; Lu et al. 2019). While some studies report positive out - comes (e.g., Feld et al. 2018; Li et al. 2018), others find minimal or no improvements beyond the local habitat scale (e.g., Verdonschot et al. 2016; White et al. 2017). This inconsistency highlights a significant challenge: despite substantial advances in wastewater treatment and water quality, hydromorphological restoration often falls short of achieving ecological recovery.

nodes.question: What role do biotic interactions play in recovery trajectories according to recent research in freshwater systems?
nodes.answer: Biotic interactions, particularly competition, play a critical role in shaping recovery trajectories by limiting recolonization success and influencing community dynamics.
nodes.paragraph: 2016; Thomp - son et al. 2018), while the significance of dispersal dur - ing recovery has also been noted (Brederveld et al. 2011; Enss et al. 2024; Gillmann et al. 2024b; Li et al. 2016; Louhi et al. 2011). Recent research in freshwater systems has also highlighted the critical role of biotic interac - tions, particularly competition, in shaping recovery tra - jectories. Brettschneider et al. (2023) and White et al. (2021) illustrate how interspecific competition can limit recolonization success and influence community dynam - ics. White et al. (2021) demonstrated that priority effects in restored streams, where established species restrict the colonization success of more vulnerable taxa, can act as a barrier to biotic recovery. Similarly, Brettschneider et al. (2023) highlight that even when habitat conditions improve, recovery may remain limited if biotic interac - tions constrain recolonization. These findings align with those of Gillmann et al. (2024a), who observed competi - tion becoming more pronounced as ecosystems recover from disturbances.
